query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear performance of high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings is governed by the in situ formation of a self-adaptive, protective oxide tribolayer during sliding wear, which reduces friction and limits material removal.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating with a near-equiatomic, nanocrystalline structure designed to promote balanced oxidation behavior.
generation.intervention: Reduce the concentration of one or more key oxidation-prone elements (e.g., lowering chromium content) in the alloy composition to disrupt the formation of the protective oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Reciprocating sliding wear test conducted in air at elevated temperatures (e.g., 300°C) under controlled stress/load conditions typical for wear-resistant applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and stability of a nanostructured oxide tribolayer on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: During wear at elevated temperatures, the original HEA composition promotes a controlled oxidation that creates a continuous, self-lubricating oxide film. This film acts as a barrier to further wear and reduces the friction coefficient. When the key oxidation-prone element is lowered, the oxide film is either not fully developed or is unstable, leading to increased friction and accelerated material removal.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the specified conditions, the baseline HEA coatings will form a robust oxide tribolayer resulting in lower wear rates and friction values. In contrast, the modified alloy with reduced oxidation-prone elements will show diminished or discontinuous oxide formation, resulting in higher wear rates and increased friction.
generation.baseline: Wear performance of the HEA coating with the full, balanced elemental composition under the same test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism should hold over the temperature range of approximately 200–400°C and under stress/load conditions common to wear-resistant applications. Deviations might occur at temperatures or loads significantly outside this range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact compositional thresholds required to alter oxide film stability, the interplay between mechanical wear and chemical oxidation, and potential contributions from other microstructural features require further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) HEA coatings with the standard, balanced composition and (2) HEA coatings with a reduced concentration of a key oxidation-promoting element (e.g., chromium). Subject both sets to reciprocating sliding wear tests in air at an elevated temperature of around 300°C under identical load and stress conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (via mass loss or profilometry)
Surface oxide layer thickness and continuity (using SEM/EDS or XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified HEA (with reduced oxidation element) exhibits a similar or lower wear rate, friction coefficient, and comparable oxide tribolayer characteristics relative to the baseline HEA, then the hypothesis that the protective effect is mediated primarily by the controlled formation of an oxide tribolayer would be falsified.
